newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINLAND BANK ACT NEEDS TWO-THIRDS MAJORITY - PAPER.
newsitem.headline: FINLAND BANK ACT NEEDS TWO-THIRDS MAJORITY - PAPER.

text.p: Parliament's constitutional committee will rule that a revision of legislation governing the Bank of Finland should be enacted by two-thirds majority, daily Helsingin Sanomat reported on Thursday.
"According to parliament's constitutional committee, the Bank of Finland proposal cannot be approved in its entirety by simple majority," the paper said.

In a statement due today the committee will state that stripping the central bank's parliamentary supervisors of their role in monetary policy decision-making will require a two-thirds majority in parliament to become law, it said.
The committee's decision, which cannot be overruled, is against the government's view, the paper noted.
The outcome marks a setback for the government's drive to adapt Bank of Finland legislation to the requirements of a European Central Bank (ECB).

The ongoing second stage of European economic and monetary union (EMU) requires EU countries to grant their central banks independence before the planned start of ECB operations in the summer of 1998.
The left-right-green cabinet may find it hard to get two-thirds MPs behind the bill, political analysts have said.

The five cabinet parties have 142 MPs in the 200-seat house where the speaker does not vote, and need 133 votes to be assured of victory. In a February 28 vote of confidence, 17 coalition party MPs voted against the government.

The controversial item in the central bank reform package is a transfer of all monetary and exchange rate policy decisions to the Bank's board of management, depriving the parliamentary supervisors of their minor but key role.
Critisising the proposed reform, opposition MPs and some MPs from governing parties have said it would remove all political influence over monetary policy decisions.
Some have claimed the sole purpose is to make sure that Finland qualifies for the third stage of EMU.

Plenary debate and voting on the Bank of Finland reform is due later this spring after parliament's economic committee completes its statement on the proposal. --Helsinki newsroom +358-9-680 50 245, e-mail news@reuters.fi
